translations.translation: With the help of Heaven.
On the eve of the 13th of Tishrei,
the yahrtzeit of the Rebbe Maharash,
the year 5748.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that "Borei Niv Sefatayim" refers to speech that comes spontaneously, which is a greater level than deliberate speech, being a true novelty.

translations.translation: "Borei niv sefatayim shalom shalom larachok v'lakarov amar Hashem v'erpateihu" (Creating the utterance of the lips, peace, peace to the far and to the near, said Hashem, and I will heal him).
And my father-in-law, the Rebbe, precisely notes in his maamar beginning with these words, said on the 13th of Tishrei fifty years ago,
that "niv sefatayim" is speech that comes by itself
[for the meaning of the term "niv sefatayim" is that the utterance
(speech)
comes from the lips themselves,
meaning that the speech is not through thought and intention, but rather comes on its own],
and what is the virtue of speech that comes by itself.
And to add,
that the language of the verse is "Borei niv sefatayim,"
for the explanation of "creation" (beriah) is a novelty (chiddush),
that a new thing is made that did not exist before,
similar to the novelty of yesh mei'ayin (existence from nothing).
[For although the term "creation" also applies to a coming-into-being of yesh mi'yesh (existence from existence),
as is also understood from the fact that everything that came into being during the six days of creation
(even the particular creations that came into being after the first day of Ma'aseh Bereishit,
even though they came into being from the heavens and the earth that were created on the first day of Ma'aseh Bereishit)
is called by the name "creation,"
and as it is written,
"And Elokim created (vayivra) the man, etc.,"
even though the body of man was formed from dust,
and also regarding the soul of man it is written,
"And He blew into his nostrils the soul of life,"
for blowing is not a creation of yesh mei'ayin, but rather a drawing down of the breath that existed previously,
yesh mi'yesh,
[and it is noteworthy,
that the "yesh" from which the soul comes into being is true existence,
for "one who blows, blows from within him,"
and "within him"
(His innermost and pnimiyus)
is true existence],

nevertheless, this that the term "creation" applies to a coming-into-being of yesh mi'yesh is specifically regarding a coming-into-being that is in a manner of novelty, even to the point of the novelty that is similar to the novelty of yesh mei'ayin].
And from the fact that it is written "Borei niv sefatayim,"
that "niv sefatayim" is a novelty,
it is proven,
that the superiority of "niv sefatayim,"
speech that comes by itself,
over speech that is through thought and intention,
is an incomparable superiority
(a novelty).
And it needs to be understood,
behold, speech that is through thought and intention is
(simply)
more elevated than speech that comes by itself,
and from the fact that it is written "Borei niv sefatayim" it is proven that speech that comes by itself is more elevated, even to the point of an incomparable superiority.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses the two interpretations of "far" and "near" in the verse, noting that the maamar prioritizes the Radak's geographical interpretation over the Gemara's interpretation of baalei teshuvah and tzaddikim.

translations.translation: B)
And the maamar continues,
that in the commentary of the Radak on the verse, there are two explanations of "larachok v'lakarov" (to the far and to the near).
The Radak himself explains "to the far" from Jerusalem and "to the near" to it,
and afterwards he brings that our Sages, of blessed memory, explained that "to the far" are baalei teshuvah (penitents) and "to the near" are tzaddikim (righteous).
And as it is brought in the Gemara,
"In the place where baalei teshuvah stand, even completely righteous tzaddikim cannot stand,
as it is said, 'Peace, peace to the far and to the near,'
to the far first and then to the near."
And it needs to be understood,

that from the fact that the maamar first presents the Radak's explanation before the Gemara's explanation, it implies that for the matter explained in the maamar, the Radak's explanation is more relevant,
and this requires explanation,
for in the maamar it speaks about the matter of the superiority of the baal teshuvah over tzaddikim
(as will be explained later),
so why does it first present the Radak's explanation that "to the far" is far from Jerusalem before the Gemara's explanation that "to the far" is baalei teshuvah.
